areas.name: 0 · Client framing & scope
areas.note: Document-level wording. Triggered by whether the advice request marks the client NEW or EXISTING, and which areas are scoped in/out.

scenarios.strat: [Name], you have sought advice as you would like to [opening goal — e.g. plan for a comfortable retirement and create additional passive income to support your lifestyle].

[Name], you are a current client of My Wealth Solutions and have sought further advice to review and enhance your existing strategies as you continue progressing toward your financial freedom goal.

areas.name: 1 · Debt Management
areas.note: Standard offset/surplus/tax wording is always-on when debt is scoped; the rest are tailored modules triggered by keywords. Gearing wording (term loan / equity release) only appears when a gearing strategy is scoped.

scenarios.name: Establish or utilise an offset account
scenarios.strat: We recommend you [establish / utilise] an offset account against your home loan and hold your cash and surplus within it.
scenarios.outcome: Directing your surplus income towards your existing home loan offset will save you an estimated $XX in interest costs and reduce the repayment period on your loan from XX to XX years.
why: An offset account will allow you to reduce your current interest payments but still provide you the flexibility to withdraw these funds for your liquidity needs.
The offset account use will provide estimated interest savings of $XXX over the life of the loan compared to repayment over the regular term.
risks: The effectiveness of an offset account depends on maintaining a sufficient cash balance. Withdrawing funds from the offset will increase the interest payable on your loan.
Holding funds in an offset account may result in lower investment returns than investing those funds in growth assets over the long term.
alts: Direct your surplus cashflow to a high interest savings account or a term deposit account. I discounted this strategy as you will yield a high effective after tax return by directing your surplus to your offset account (estimated to be approximately X.XX% based on your current home loan interest rate). This also allows you to reduce your bad debt at a faster rate.

We considered making additional home loan repayments instead of utilising your existing offset account, however we discounted this strategy as your offset account will provide you with flexible access to your funds, should you need to draw upon these at any point.

scenarios.name: Direct surplus income to offset
scenarios.strat: We recommend you direct your surplus income of $___ to your home loan offset account.

scenarios.name: Direct tax savings to offset
scenarios.strat: We recommend you direct your tax savings of $___ to your home loan offset account.

scenarios.name: Use cash / sale proceeds to reduce the home loan
scenarios.strat: We recommend using {amt} from your existing cash or sale proceeds to reduce your home loan.
scenarios.outcome: Paying down your home loan will release available equity for investment opportunities while reducing your minimum loan repayments, improving your ongoing cashflow.
why: Reducing non‑deductible (bad) debt improves your cashflow and releases equity for future investment.
risks: Applying cash to debt reduction may reduce your available liquidity and emergency funds. It may also limit your ability to access these funds without further borrowing.
alts: We considered retaining your available cash rather than reducing your home loan. This was not recommended as reducing your home loan improves your cash flow, reduces interest costs and/or provides greater flexibility to implement your investment strategy.

scenarios.name: Retain an emergency cash buffer in the offset
scenarios.strat: We recommend retaining {amt} in your offset account as an emergency cash buffer.
scenarios.outcome: Retaining cash in your home loan offset account provides a readily accessible emergency reserve while continuing to reduce the interest payable on your home loan.
why: Maintains accessible funds for emergencies while still reducing home loan interest.
risks: Holding funds in an offset account may result in lower investment returns than investing those funds in growth assets over the long term.

scenarios.name: Consolidate car loan into home loan
scenarios.strat: We recommend consolidating your existing car loan into your home loan.
scenarios.outcome: Consolidating your car loan into your home loan will reduce your overall borrowing costs by replacing higher-interest debt with lower-interest home loan debt, while simplifying the management of your debts.
why: Replaces higher‑interest short‑term debt with lower‑interest home loan debt and simplifies your lending.
risks: While this may reduce your interest rate and repayments, extending short-term debt over a longer home loan term could result in paying more total interest if additional repayments are not made.
alts: We considered retaining your existing car loan. This was not recommended as consolidating your debt reduces interest costs and simplifies your lending arrangements.

scenarios.name: Consolidate other debt (personal loan / credit card)
scenarios.strat: We recommend you clear your credit card / personal loan balance using funds from your home loan offset account, and close the facility to prevent re-accumulation.
scenarios.outcome: High-interest consumer debt is repaid using lower-cost funds, and the facility is closed to stop it building up again.
why: Credit cards and personal loans typically carry far higher interest than your home loan; clearing them removes that high-cost interest.
Closing the facility removes the temptation to re-borrow.
risks: If the facility is not closed, the balance can re-accumulate; closing a card may briefly affect your credit score.
alts: Maintain minimum repayments on the existing facility — discounted as it leaves high-interest debt in place.

scenarios.name: Refinance investment property loan from P&I to interest only
scenarios.strat: We recommend refinancing your investment property loan from principal and interest to interest only repayments.
scenarios.outcome: Switching your investment property loan from principal and interest to interest-only repayments will improve your short-term cash flow. Following the debt restructure, surplus funds can be redirected towards other wealth creation opportunities.
why: Improves short‑term cashflow and frees surplus for other wealth‑creation opportunities.
risks: Interest only repayments do not reduce the loan principal, meaning the outstanding balance will remain unchanged and total interest paid over the life of the loan may be higher.
alts: We considered retaining principal and interest repayments. This was not recommended as interest-only repayments improve short-term cash flow, allowing surplus funds to be directed towards other wealth creation opportunities.

scenarios.name: Refinance to draw on available equity (GEARING)
scenarios.gate: Only if a gearing strategy is scoped
scenarios.strat: We recommend you refinance your existing home and/or investment property loan to draw on your available equity.
scenarios.outcome: Your home loan will be split into tax deductible and non-deductible components, increasing your tax efficiency.
why: Refinance of your existing loan structure to use available equity will allow you to begin investing more now as opposed to waiting until the loan is fully repaid.
Replaces “bad” (non tax deductible) debt with “good” (tax deductible) investment debt.
risks: (uses the standard gearing risk list — see Term Loan / debt recycling)
alts: (uses the gearing alternatives — see Investment Plan)

scenarios.name: Use equity to fund the 20% deposit for an investment property purchase (GEARING)
scenarios.gate: Only if an IP purchase funded by equity is scoped
scenarios.strat: We recommend you use the equity to fund the 20% deposit (plus costs) for an investment property purchase.
scenarios.outcome: (outcome carried by the Investment Property section)
why: Allows you to acquire a growth asset now using available equity rather than waiting to accumulate a cash deposit.
risks: (uses the standard gearing risk list)

scenarios.name: Establish a Term Loan / debt recycling (GEARING)
scenarios.gate: Only if a gearing strategy is scoped
scenarios.strat:
We recommend you establish a Term Loan for investment purposes using your existing home or investment property loan as equity.
We recommend you utilise the offset account against your home mortgage.
scenarios.outcome: A debt recycling strategy essentially converts your non tax deductible (home loan) debt into tax deductible investment debt over a period of time.
why: Many people wait until their home loan is repaid before starting to invest. A strategy that lets you invest now and continue to pay off your home loan reasonably quickly is called debt recycling. It involves three key steps: use your home equity as security for a separate investment loan; use any tax savings (and surplus cash flow) to reduce your outstanding home loan balance; re‑borrow from your investment loan the amount you have paid off your home loan to purchase additional investments.
Refinance of your existing loan structure to use available equity will allow you to begin investing more now as opposed to waiting until the loan is fully repaid.
Replaces “bad” (non tax deductible) debt with “good” (tax deductible) investment debt.
Allows for your home loan to be repaid in approximately XX years instead of XX years.
Allows you to utilise your Term Loan to invest in assets sooner than would have otherwise been possible.

Additional Benefits: Interest on investment debt provides ongoing tax deductions, reducing the amount of interest you pay. Debt recycling helps to establish an investment portfolio sooner and allows a portfolio to realise long term growth.
risks: You remain liable for the principal borrowed, irrespective of the performance of your investment portfolio;
There is the risk of the lender having recourse to the home used as security, and therefore the risk of losing the home;

If interest rates increase your interest payments will increase accordingly, requiring additional cash. Gearing increases the risk attached to a portfolio, as gearing will magnify both gains and losses;
Gearing is inappropriate for people without satisfactory cash flow/income to meet borrowing costs;
While gearing enhances your potential for bigger gains, it can also expose you to a greater risk in a falling market;
Assets purchased with borrowed funds may actually fall in value. This means that although you might receive extra tax deductions over time, you might actually lose funds;
Due to the high risk nature of a gearing strategy, I recommend that you review the suitability of your leveraged portfolio on at least an annual basis;

A gearing strategy requires a long term investment horizon. Investment returns can be volatile, and in order to withstand short term fluctuations, I recommend a minimum 5 year investment time horizon;
alts: We considered restructuring all of your lending to interest only loans and making additional salary sacrifice contributions to super for the difference you were paying on your home loan principal. I have discounted this strategy because home ownership is a higher priority for you than growing your superannuation at this time and you wish to take advantage of a debt recycling strategy to reduce your “bad” non tax deductible debt within your existing loan account and pay your home off as soon as possible.

scenarios.name: Use inheritance / windfall to pay down the home loan
scenarios.strat: We recommend you use $XXX of your anticipated inheritance to pay down your home loan [after your fixed rate has expired], and retain $XXX of your inheritance in your offset account to cover [expected home renovations / an emergency buffer].
scenarios.outcome: Applying your inheritance to your home loan reduces non-deductible debt and interest cost, while retaining a portion in offset keeps funds accessible for planned expenses.
why: Reduces bad (non-deductible) debt, improving cashflow and bringing forward the date your home loan is repaid.
Retaining a portion in the offset keeps funds accessible for planned costs (e.g. renovations) while still reducing home loan interest.
risks: Applying funds to debt reduces your available liquidity; retaining an appropriate offset buffer mitigates this.
If a fixed rate applies, break costs may arise from paying down before the fixed term expires — time the repayment for after the fixed rate expires.
alts: Invest the inheritance instead of reducing the home loan — discounted where reducing non-deductible debt provides a certain, tax-effective return equal to your home loan rate.

scenarios.name: Switch investment property loan(s) from principal & interest to interest only
triggers: switch home loan to interest only
scenarios.strat: We recommend you switch your investment property loan(s) from principal & interest to interest only to improve cashflow and maintain tax-deductible debt.
scenarios.outcome: Switching to interest-only repayments improves your short-term cash flow, freeing surplus to direct towards your investment strategy or offset.
why: Improves short-term cashflow, freeing surplus for other wealth-creation opportunities or to hold in offset.
risks: Interest only repayments do not reduce the loan principal, so the outstanding balance remains unchanged and total interest paid over the life of the loan may be higher.
Interest on your home loan is not tax deductible, so interest-only on non-deductible debt should be used with a clear plan to reduce the principal.
alts: Retain principal and interest repayments — discounted where the cashflow freed up is better directed to your investment strategy or offset.

scenarios.name: Sell current home and purchase a new home (PPR — set aside funds)
scenarios.strat: You intend to sell your current home. As this is your principal residence we do not provide advice on it; we recommend you set aside $___ to fund the purchase of your new home.
scenarios.outcome: Your move to the new home is funded with an equity-drawdown deposit now, then tidied up with the sale proceeds, and your debt and cashflow are restructured around the upgraded home.
why: Setting aside the required funds ensures the purchase of your next home is covered from sale proceeds and available cash.
risks: Sale price and timing are uncertain; transaction costs (agent, legal, stamp duty) apply.

areas.name: 2 · Investment Property
areas.note: Existing or proposed. The purchase‑using‑equity wording is verbatim from your SOAs; the event scenarios (sell‑to‑buy, upgrade, convert to IP, downsizer) are my drafts for your review.

scenarios.name: Purchase an investment property using equity
scenarios.strat:
We recommend you purchase an investment property (in the name of [owner]) to the value of approximately $XXX (plus costs).
We recommend the loan for the investment property should be Interest Only.
We recommend you arrange for all property costs and property loan repayments to come out of the ICA, and for the rental income to be paid into the ICA.
scenarios.outcome: Our projections indicate this strategy may generate additional wealth of approximately $XXX over the term (estimated at XX years).
why: Builds a long-term growth investment outside of the super environment and share market providing long term diversification for your investment portfolio.

Additional Benefits: As a growth asset, an investment property provides a combination of long-term investment income and capital growth, as well as ongoing tax deductions. Property can be less volatile than shares and/or other investments.
risks: There is the risk of the lender having recourse to the home used as security, and therefore the risk of losing the home;
If interest rates increase your interest payments will increase accordingly. Gearing increases the risk attached to a property, as gearing will magnify both gains and losses;
The return on the investment (rent) may decrease or temporarily cease, which may place some strain on your cash flow;
A gearing strategy requires a long term investment horizon. I recommend a minimum 5 year investment time horizon;
alts: Direct additional funds to Australian shares instead of purchasing an investment property. I have discounted this strategy as shares may require a high level of ongoing monitoring... and your managed fund already has an allocation to Australian shares so allocating additional funds may concentrate your portfolio excessively within the one asset class.

Direct additional funds to your superannuation account instead of purchasing an investment property. I have discounted this strategy, as funds in superannuation are not generally accessible unless specific conditions of release are met...

While we do not give specific advice on which property to purchase, we provide purchase criteria and can assist you to locate an appropriately licenced real estate agent / buyer's advocate. Alternatively, you may wish to source the property yourself.

scenarios.name: Purchase an investment property using cash / savings
scenarios.strat: We recommend you purchase an investment property to the value of approximately $XXX (plus costs), funded from your available cash/savings.
scenarios.outcome: Our projections indicate this strategy may generate additional wealth of approximately $XXX over the term.
why: Builds a long‑term growth investment outside super, diversifying your portfolio, without taking on additional borrowings.
risks: Property is an illiquid asset; you may be unable to access funds quickly if needed.
The return on the investment (rent) may decrease or temporarily cease.
alts: Direct the funds to your investment portfolio or superannuation instead — discounted for the reasons noted in the Investment Plan alternatives.

scenarios.name: Sell current property and use proceeds to buy a new property
scenarios.strat: We recommend you sell your existing property at [address] for an estimated $XXX and use the net proceeds to purchase a new property to the value of approximately $XXX (plus costs).
scenarios.outcome: Realising your existing property allows you to reposition into a property better aligned with your goals while managing your overall borrowings.
why: Allows you to reposition into a more suitable property/location aligned to your goals.
Net sale proceeds reduce the borrowings required for the new purchase.
risks: Selling will trigger transaction costs (agent fees, legals) and may crystallise capital gains tax.
Timing risk between sale and purchase; you may require bridging finance.
alts: Retain the existing property and borrow separately for the new purchase — discounted where servicing two loans is not appropriate for your cashflow.

scenarios.name: Convert current home into an investment property
scenarios.strat: We recommend you retain your existing home and convert it into an investment property, renting it at an estimated $XXX per week.
scenarios.outcome: Converting your home to an investment property retains a growth asset and creates a new source of rental income and tax deductions.
why: Retains a growth asset you know well and creates rental income.
Interest on the loan (to the extent it relates to the income‑producing use) may become tax deductible.
risks: The deductibility of interest depends on the use of the borrowed funds, not the security — obtain advice from your accountant.
As a former home, capital gains tax may apply on a future sale (subject to the 6‑year absence rule).
Rental income may decrease or temporarily cease.
alts: Sell the existing home and invest the proceeds — discounted where retaining the property better meets your long‑term goals.

scenarios.name: Retain an existing investment property
scenarios.strat: We recommend you retain your existing investment property for now. Where a sale is intended, we recommend timing it to occur after your fund has commenced pension phase to minimise capital gains tax, and directing the proceeds to fund your retirement income.
scenarios.outcome: The property is retained and, if sold, the sale is timed for the pension phase to reduce or remove CGT, with proceeds funding your income.
why: Retaining the property preserves the asset and rental income; timing any eventual sale to the pension phase reduces the CGT payable on the gain.
risks: Property is illiquid and concentrated; market timing on any sale is uncertain; confirm the tax treatment with your accountant.
alts: Sell the property now — discounted where deferring the sale to pension phase materially reduces CGT.

scenarios.name: Sell an existing investment property
scenarios.strat: We recommend you sell your existing investment property at [address] for an estimated $XXX and redeploy the net proceeds as set out in this advice.
scenarios.outcome: Realising the property frees capital to redeploy into a more suitable, diversified and liquid strategy.
why: Frees capital for a more diversified/liquid strategy aligned to your goals.
Reduces concentration and gearing risk.
risks: The sale will trigger transaction costs and may crystallise capital gains tax — consult your accountant.
You forgo future rental income and any further capital growth on the property.
alts: Retain the property — discounted where it no longer suits your goals or cashflow.

scenarios.name: Downsizer (sell home, downsize, contribute proceeds)
scenarios.strat: You have advised you have sold (or intend to sell) your home and would like to use the proceeds to assist in funding your retirement. We recommend you downsize and direct the proceeds to superannuation via the downsizer contribution.
scenarios.outcome: Selling and downsizing frees up capital from your home which is redirected into super to fund retirement, without affecting your existing Centrelink entitlements where confirmed.
why: Downsizing releases equity tied up in your home and, via the downsizer contribution, moves it into the tax-effective super environment to fund a retirement income stream.
risks: Selling and buying incurs transaction costs (agent, legal, stamp duty); proceeds in super are preserved; the home sale and any new purchase must be timed carefully.
alts: Retain the home and draw on other assets — discounted where releasing home equity is needed to fund retirement.

areas.name: 3 · Investment Bond
areas.note: Investment bond strategies + product, separate from the investment plan.

scenarios.name: Investment bond
scenarios.gate: Investment bond scoped (commonly for children's education / high-income earners)
scenarios.strat:
We recommend you establish [a new investment bond / two new investment bonds for each of your children] through the Generation Life – Life Builder Investment Bond platform and invest in line with your risk profile.
You will be able to nominate [child/beneficiary] as the beneficiary of this account.
We recommend you invest the funds into the following investment options: [e.g. Vanguard Growth Portfolio – 100%].
scenarios.outcome: An investment bond provides a tax-effective, long-term structure (earnings taxed within the bond at a maximum of 30%, with no tax payable on withdrawals subject to the 10-year rule), ideal for accumulating for your children's future.
why: Earnings within the bond are taxed at a maximum of 30% (not your marginal rate), and there is no tax payable on future withdrawals subject to the 10-year rule.
You can nominate your child / beneficiary on the account, making it a tax-effective vehicle to accumulate for their future (e.g. education).
The recommended index funds aim to track particular market indices — a passive, cost-effective way to gain broad, diversified market exposure, reducing overall risk.
risks: If you withdraw part or all of your investment bond prior to the 10th year, some of the profits will be assessable to you, although you will receive a 30% tax offset equal to the assessable amount.

If you contribute more than 125% of the previous year's contributions, the 10-year period will restart (this applies where, for example, you make no contribution in a year and then later look to make further contributions).
You may pay a buy/sell spread and switching fees; there are fees and costs associated with using an investment bond.

Investment bonds involve some investment risk and do not guarantee your returns; values may fall. By investing instead of holding cash you lose capital stability and access to the government deposit guarantee up to $250,000.
alts: Hold the funds in cash (a cash management trust or savings account) for your children — discounted as, over the medium to long term, a managed investment provides greater opportunity for capital growth than holding cash.

Invest via an ordinary investment platform for your children — discounted as you would not receive the same tax benefits (earnings taxed at a maximum of 30% and no tax payable on future withdrawals, subject to the 10-year rule).
We completed a price comparison between Generation Life, Australian Unity and Centuria investment bonds. Generation Life was the most cost-effective platform.

areas.name: 4 · Investment Plan
areas.note: Regular investment / debt recycling wording is verbatim. Investment bond, lump‑sum and inheritance variants are drafts for your review (no investment‑bond example in these five SOAs — please send one).

scenarios.name: Lump-sum investment
scenarios.strat: We recommend you invest a lump sum of $XXX into a new investment account and invest in line with your risk profile.
scenarios.outcome: Our projections indicate this strategy may generate additional wealth of $XXX over the term.
why: Puts surplus capital to work in a diversified, professionally managed portfolio you can access outside super.
Reinvesting distributions accelerates growth through compounding.
risks: Investment funds involve some investment risk and do not guarantee your returns; values may fall.
By investing instead of holding cash you lose capital stability and the deposit guarantee up to $250,000.
alts: Hold the funds in cash/term deposit — discounted as it yields a lower long‑term return and does not meet your wealth‑creation goal.
Contribute to superannuation instead — discounted as super is not accessible until a condition of release is met.

scenarios.name: In-specie transfer — retain existing holdings in the new platform (no sale)
scenarios.strat: We recommend you in-specie transfer your existing portfolio into the new account and retain the holdings (no sale), avoiding CGT and transaction costs.
scenarios.outcome: Transferring your holdings in‑specie retains your investments while bringing them under professional management, with internal netting used to reduce transaction costs and CGT.
why: Retains your existing holdings while bringing them under the recommended professionally managed portfolio.
Internal netting with the CARE portfolio reduces transaction costs and potential capital gains tax.
risks: As part of the rebalance into the CARE portfolio, the remaining assets that cannot be internally netted may need to be sold down, which may crystallise an estimated capital gain of $XXX and an estimated tax liability of approximately $XXX. Please consult an accountant to confirm the tax implications and ensure sufficient cash reserves are available.
alts: Sell the entire portfolio and re‑invest the cash — discounted as the in‑specie transfer with internal netting reduces transaction costs and CGT.

scenarios.name: Use inheritance / windfall to invest
scenarios.strat: We recommend you invest your inheritance of {amt} into a new investment account, invested in line with your risk profile, and elect to reinvest distributions.
scenarios.outcome: Investing your inheritance puts the capital to work in a diversified, professionally managed portfolio aligned to your goals.
why: Puts a windfall to work toward your long‑term goals in a diversified, accessible portfolio.
risks: Investment funds involve investment risk; values may fall. You lose capital stability vs holding cash.
alts: Use the inheritance to reduce non‑deductible debt instead — see Debt. Discounted where building investment assets better meets the goal.

scenarios.name: Sell down an existing investment / asset
scenarios.strat: We recommend you sell down your existing [Hub24 Investment Account / share portfolio].
scenarios.outcome: Selling down your existing portfolio consolidates your assets into a more streamlined structure, reducing administration and management complexity and costs; after the sell-down you will no longer be liable to pay tax on future investment earnings on those assets.
why: Consolidates assets into a more streamlined structure across superannuation and cash holdings, reducing ongoing administration and management costs.
risks: As a result of the sell down, you will crystallise a capital gain of approximately $XXX and capital gains tax of approximately $XXX. Please consult with your accountant to understand your tax liability prior to implementing this advice.
There is a risk of being temporarily out of market between selling your existing investments and reinvesting, which could result in missed market returns during this period.
alts: Retain the existing arrangement — discounted where consolidating simplifies administration and improves the overall structure.

scenarios.name: Vanguard index option (instead of CARE managed portfolios)
scenarios.strat: We recommend you establish a new [Hub24] investment account and transfer your existing CARE investment holdings to the Vanguard [Diversified Balanced] Portfolio. Investments common to both portfolios will be transferred via in-specie; assets not available within the Vanguard portfolio will be sold and the proceeds reinvested into the recommended portfolio.
scenarios.outcome: A passive index approach gives broad, low-cost diversified market exposure, minimising turnover so you can take advantage of available capital gains tax concessions.
why: The recommended index funds aim to track the performance of particular market indices. Index funds are a passive, cost-effective way to gain exposure to the market and provide broad diversification, reducing your overall risk.

Vanguard index funds reduce the tracking-error risk of a portfolio by holding most index securities very close to their index weights, providing truly diversified market exposure at a lower investment cost than your managed fund.
An index management approach minimises portfolio turnover so investors can take advantage of available capital gains tax concessions.
risks: A passive index approach does not seek to outperform the market and will move with it, including in falling markets.
Index funds carry the normal market and investment risks; values may fall.
alts: While the recommended Vanguard [High Growth] Index Fund has higher ongoing management fees than the iShares Enhanced Strategic Growth Fund, the iShares manager has yet to demonstrate an ability to consistently add value, and the iShares fund would expose your portfolio to fund-manager risk whereas the Vanguard index fund does not.
Retain the CARE actively managed portfolio — discounted where the client prefers a lower-cost passive index approach.

scenarios.name: Money on the move — tactical dollar-cost averaging acceleration
scenarios.figures: 1 month of DCA brought forward per 5% market drop
scenarios.strat: As per the money-on-the-move framework, for every 5% drop in the market we may bring forward one month's dollar-cost averaging to ensure your funds are invested as efficiently as possible.
scenarios.outcome: Capital is deployed faster during market falls, improving the average entry price across your dollar-cost-averaging program.
why: Bringing forward scheduled investments during market falls allows you to invest at lower prices, improving long-term efficiency of the dollar-cost-averaging approach.
risks: Markets may fall further after funds are deployed; accelerating investment increases short-term exposure to further declines.
The framework is a guideline applied at our discretion, not a guarantee of improved returns.
alts: Maintain a fixed dollar-cost-averaging schedule regardless of market movements — discounted as it forgoes the opportunity to invest at lower prices during falls.

scenarios.name: Establish a new investment account
scenarios.gate: Couple establishing a non-super investment account together
scenarios.strat: We recommend you establish a new investment account and invest in line with your risk profile.
scenarios.outcome: A single jointly-held portfolio simplifies administration and estate transfer between you.
why: Joint ownership simplifies estate transfer (the account passes to the survivor) and supports a unified investment plan for the household.
risks: A joint account exposes the full balance to either party's creditors and is treated as a shared asset on separation.
Income and capital gains are split per ownership, which may not be the most tax-effective split if your incomes differ materially.
alts: Hold separate individual accounts (cleaner separation) or invest in the lower-income earner's name (more tax-effective) — chosen approach reflects your preference for a shared plan.

scenarios.name: Reserves & cash buffer for tactical liquidity (avoid forced selling)
scenarios.gate: Investment / pension portfolio where a cash/reserves sleeve is held
scenarios.strat: We recommend you set aside funds in Reserves & Cash to provide you with liquidity and low volatility, so you shouldn't have to sell growth assets through necessity or bad decisions during downturns.
scenarios.outcome: A reserves sleeve funds your needs through market falls, so growth assets are not sold at the wrong time.
why: Holding a low-volatility reserve protects you from forced sales at market troughs and preserves your growth assets to recover.
You rebalance by topping up reserves from growth assets as part of your annual review.

The reserve can be phased to your circumstances — e.g. hold a reduced reserve (1.5 years instead of the usual 2.5 years of pension requirements) where known cash inflows such as upcoming property sales are due, then restore it, reviewed each year.
risks: Holding reserves creates a return drag during strong markets; the allocation must be rebalanced to stay aligned with your risk profile.
alts: Remain fully invested for higher expected return — discounted as it exposes you to forced selling in downturns.

scenarios.name: Regular investment from cashflow (initial + ongoing)
