areas.name: 5 · Personal Superannuation
areas.note: Rollover variants, defined benefit and SMSF wording are verbatim from your SOAs. Military super and pension/TTR variants are drafts.

scenarios.name: Establish new fund + full rollover (close & transfer 100%)
triggers: rollover full benefits to new fund
scenarios.strat:
[Name], we recommend you close your existing [Fund] and transfer 100% of the balance to a new fund that has been customised for your needs.
[Name], we recommend that you provide your employer with the details of your new superannuation fund to ensure all future contributions are directed to your new account.
scenarios.outcome: Your superannuation strategies will be professionally managed in a way to maximise your superannuation benefits and stay in line with your needs. We estimate your new fund to have a total balance of approximately $XXX in XX years' time.
why: Your superannuation will be invested in line with your risk profile and will help you achieve your goal of maximising your superannuation for retirement while being managed on your behalf.
Increased investment choice, which provides your adviser with the ability to tailor your investment portfolio to your long term investment strategy.
Achieve your goal of partially funding adviser fees from superannuation and the ability to maintain ongoing advice.

Seamless transfer from accumulation to pension (not required to sell down your assets to transfer into the pension phase). This can prevent unnecessary Capital Gains Tax consequences and/or sale of assets at a time of unfavourable market conditions.
risks: Generally, any money held within superannuation is not accessible until retirement.
Depending on the components that make up your superannuation benefits, withdrawing money before age 60 may result in lump sum tax being payable.
When you die, the proceeds from your superannuation fund may be subject to lump sum tax if paid to non-dependants.
There may be transaction costs involved in establishing the strategy.
alts: Rollover part of your super in order to retain your existing insurance cover within super. I have discounted this strategy as the recommended replacement insurance cover provides additional benefits (such as improved definitions and access to trauma insurance)... a partial rollover would also mean more than one super account, which makes keeping track of your super more difficult.
Retain your existing super accounts. I discounted this strategy as your existing super account has limited functionality for your adviser to easily manage your superannuation on your behalf.

scenarios.name: Establish new fund + partial rollover, retain minimum for insurance
scenarios.strat: [Name], we recommend you retain the minimum required ($XXX) in your existing [Fund] to retain your underwritten [Life & TPD] insurance and transfer the remaining balance to a new fund that has been customised for your needs. [Name], we recommend that you continue to direct your super guarantee to your existing [Fund] account and we recommend making annual partial rollovers to your new fund.
scenarios.outcome: Retaining your existing fund allows you to keep your underwritten insurance cover while moving the balance to a professionally managed fund.
why: Retaining your [Fund] will allow you to retain your underwritten insurance cover.
Seamless transfer from accumulation to pension... prevents unnecessary Capital Gains Tax consequences and/or sale of assets at unfavourable market conditions.
Access to investment funds, ASX listed shares, cash and TDs, and ease of administration through consolidated reporting.

Two-stage approach: complete an initial partial rollover retaining the minimum balance (e.g. $6,000) to keep your existing insurance active; once your new cover is in place and underwritten, complete a full rollover to consolidate — this final rollover cancels the old fund's insurance.
risks: By maintaining two superannuation accounts you will incur a duplication of fees and increased administration effort to maintain your multiple accounts.
You will experience market volatility. There may be transaction costs involved in establishing the strategy.
Withdrawing money from superannuation as a lump sum before you reach age 60 may result in lump sum tax being payable.
Do not cancel the old fund's cover until the new cover is confirmed in place — if the new application is declined or modified, the old cover cannot be reinstated.
alts: [Name], we considered rolling over all of the balance and not retaining the existing insurance cover within super. I have discounted this strategy in order to maintain your insurance cover held within your existing super account.

scenarios.name: Retain existing fund (invest in line with risk profile)
triggers: retain and invest in line with risk profile
scenarios.strat: We recommend you retain your existing [Fund] Superannuation account (in line with your risk profile) that has been customised for your needs. We recommend that you continue to direct your employer contributions to your existing [Fund] account.
scenarios.outcome: Your superannuation will be invested in line with your risk profile and will help you achieve your goal of maximising your superannuation for retirement.
why: Increased investment choice, which provides your adviser with the ability to tailor your investment portfolio to your long term investment strategy.
You can fund your insurance premiums through your superannuation account as desired.
Reinvesting distributions will accelerate the growth potential and the benefits from compounding growth.
Retained to minimise crystallising capital gains tax on existing holdings.
risks: Generally, any money held within superannuation is not accessible until retirement.
The underlying investments within super involve investment risk and do not guarantee your returns; values may fall.
alts: An alternative is investing using a passive index fund approach instead of an actively managed approach like CARE. We have discounted this strategy as we believe the actively managed asset mix offered through CARE provides the optimal way to achieve your long term investment goals while minimising volatility over the short term.

scenarios.name: Consolidate multiple super accounts
scenarios.strat: We recommend you consolidate your existing superannuation accounts into a single fund customised for your needs (after confirming no valuable insurance or benefits are lost).
scenarios.outcome: Consolidating your super reduces duplicated fees and simplifies the management of your retirement savings.
why: Avoid multiple sets of fees – one fund means one set of fees.
Keep better track of your superannuation investment when it's in one place.
By having all of your super together in one account it's easier to plan for a future that includes a comfortable retirement.
risks: Having a number of superannuation plans results in additional fees, difficulty keeping track of your funds and difficulty in maintaining a suitable investment strategy — however you may lose insurance cover or benefits held in a fund being closed, so confirm before consolidating.
alts: Retain separate accounts — discounted where duplicated fees and administration outweigh any benefit of multiple funds.

scenarios.name: In-specie transfer of super holdings
scenarios.strat: We recommend completing an in-specie transfer of your [SMSF / existing] assets ([Hub24 Investment and MCMA]) into a personal superannuation fund tailored to your needs.
scenarios.outcome: An in-specie transfer keeps your portfolio invested while moving it to the recommended fund, saving transaction costs and buy/sell spreads and minimising out-of-market risk.
why: An in-specie transfer reduces the need to sell down assets, withdraw funds to your bank account, or re-purchase assets. This saves you on associated transaction costs and buy/sell spreads, and minimises out-of-market risk, ensuring your portfolios remain invested.

The recommended platform (Hub24) offers the option to in-specie transfer eligible investment options, helping you consolidate your investments into a single platform and streamline ongoing management and administration.
risks: Assets that are not eligible for in-specie transfer (or that cannot be internally netted) may need to be sold down, which may crystallise capital gains tax — consult your accountant.

scenarios.name: Retain a defined benefit fund (scope out)
scenarios.strat: [Name], we recommend you retain your existing Defined Benefit [Fund] account including the insurance arrangements held within this account. [Name], your employer superannuation contributions are required to continue to be directed to your existing defined benefit account while you remain employed in the [public sector].
scenarios.outcome: Retaining your defined benefit account preserves your guaranteed scheme benefits and existing insurance.
why: Preserves the guaranteed/defined-benefit entitlement and any valuable insurance held in the scheme.
Where the DB fund provides inbuilt Life and Income Protection benefits, these are retained as there is no premium cost charged to you for these benefits.
risks: Due to restrictions within the fund (Defined Benefit portion) — and because the benefit is determined by a formula — we are unable to make any changes or provide advice on this; it is scoped out.
Defined benefit entitlements are subject to specific scheme rules, preservation requirements and legislative considerations which differ from accumulation funds.
alts: Transfer the balance to an accumulation fund — discounted as it would forgo the valuable defined‑benefit entitlement.

scenarios.name: Retain military super (member & ancillary + employer/DB portion)
scenarios.strat: [Name], we recommend you retain your existing Military Super, including the insurance arrangements held within this account, while you remain in service. We have scoped out your Military Super (Defined Benefit portion) from this advice.
scenarios.outcome: Retaining your military super preserves the employer/defined‑benefit entitlement and any insurance, while we manage the balance of your strategy.
why: Preserves the employer/defined-benefit entitlement and any valuable insurance held in the scheme.
risks: You are required to retain the defined benefit portion in your existing Military Super fund (Employer Benefit portion) as you are unable to access this until age 55 — it is scoped out of this advice.
These funds are not accessible until a condition of release is met, nor can they be rolled over to another fund.
alts: Roll the member & ancillary balance to an accumulation fund — the employer/defined-benefit portion must be retained while in service.

scenarios.name: Redirect / continue employer contributions
scenarios.strat:
We recommend that you provide your employer with the details of your new superannuation fund to ensure all future contributions are directed to your new account.
(OR, where a fund is retained:) We recommend that you continue to direct your employer contributions to your existing [Fund].
scenarios.outcome: Ensures your employer contributions flow to the appropriate fund under the recommended strategy.
why: Keeps future contributions aligned with the recommended fund structure.

scenarios.name: Establish / set up an SMSF (and manage — rebalance + pension transition)
scenarios.strat:
We recommend you establish a new Account Based Pension account and invest in line with your risk profile.
We recommend you commence drawing an income of $XXX p.a. through your Account Based Pension account.
scenarios.outcome: We estimate your funds will sustain your desired income, making you able to draw approximately $XXX p.a. for approximately XX years.
why: Rolling over the accumulation portion to a pension account will mean all future earnings within this fund will be tax free.
Drawing an income stream will provide you with the funds required to maintain your lifestyle in line with your retirement goals.
Funding your lifestyle in this manner will ensure you're drawing down your retirement capital in the most tax efficient manner.
risks: Generally, any money held within superannuation is not accessible until retirement.
When you die, the proceeds from your superannuation fund may be subject to tax if they are paid as a lump sum to non-dependants, as defined for tax purposes.
The underlying investments within super involve some investment risk and do not guarantee your returns; values may fall.
Amounts moved to pension phase count toward your transfer balance cap; minimum annual pension payments must be drawn.
alts: Remain in accumulation phase / take a partial rollover — if a partial rollover were to take place, this would also mean you end up with more than one super account, which makes keeping track of your super more difficult over time.

scenarios.name: Commence a pension / transition to retirement (TTR)
scenarios.strat:
We recommend you establish a new Transition to Retirement (TTR) pension account through your existing [Hub24 Super] platform and invest in line with your risk profile using the CARE Philosophy.
We recommend you roll over the full balance from your existing [Fund] (Accumulation) account into your new TTR pension account.
We recommend you withdraw the maximum allowable 10% of your TTR account balance as a lump sum each financial year — approximately $XXX per annum.
scenarios.outcome: Investment earnings within a TTR account are tax-free, and as you are over age 60 all income payments from the TTR pension are also tax-free, supplementing your cashflow while you remain employed.
why: Your superannuation will be invested in line with your risk profile and will help you achieve your goal of maximising your superannuation for retirement while being managed on your behalf.
Investment earnings within a TTR account are tax-free, and as you are over age 60, all income payments received from the TTR pension will also be tax-free.
Drawing an income stream will provide you with the funds required to support your cashflow requirements.
risks: A TTR strategy is primarily designed to supplement your income while you remain employed. It should be reviewed annually to ensure it continues to meet your income needs, remains aligned with your retirement objectives, and reflects any future legislative changes affecting TTR pension rules.
Withdrawing funds now will reduce the amount available when you convert your TTR pension to a full retirement pension.
There is the normal risk of markets falling and unforeseen circumstances requiring you to draw funds when markets are down.
alts: We considered rolling over your full [existing] super account and rolling over 100% of the balance to the existing [Hub24] Super fund, however we discounted this strategy in order to maintain your insurance cover held within your existing super account.

scenarios.name: Recontribution strategy
scenarios.strat: We recommend you establish two new superannuation accounts and invest in line with your risk profile. We recommend you make a non-concessional contribution of $XXX into [Account 2] to facilitate the implementation of a recontribution strategy.
scenarios.outcome: A recontribution strategy converts a taxable component into a tax-free component, improving the tax treatment of your super death benefit for non-dependant beneficiaries.
why: Converts a taxable component to a tax-free component. A super death benefit paid to a dependant is tax free; if paid to a non-dependant, the tax payable depends on the components that make up the benefit — increasing the tax-free proportion reduces potential death benefits tax.
Can be combined with spouse equalisation to make better use of both transfer balance caps.
risks: You must have met a condition of release to withdraw; the recontribution counts toward your non-concessional cap and is preserved. Obtain advice on the tax components before implementing.
alts: Retain the existing components — discounted where improving the tax-free proportion benefits your beneficiaries.

scenarios.name: SMSF wind-up / split on separation (in-specie to personal super)
scenarios.strat: Following your separation, we recommend completing an in-specie transfer of your allocated SMSF assets into a personal superannuation fund tailored to your needs.
scenarios.outcome: Moving your allocated SMSF assets in-specie to a personal fund keeps them invested while removing the ongoing trustee obligations of the SMSF following separation.
why: Keeps your share of the assets invested while transferring them out of the SMSF, avoiding sell-down costs and out-of-market risk.
Removes the ongoing administration, audit and trustee compliance obligations of maintaining the SMSF after separation.
risks: Assets not eligible for in-specie transfer may need to be sold down, which may crystallise CGT.
SMSF wind-up has its own administrative and compliance steps; consult your accountant/SMSF administrator.
alts: Retain the SMSF — discounted where, following separation, the cost and complexity of the SMSF is no longer appropriate.

scenarios.name: Disability super benefit — staged lump-sum withdrawals (TPD/disability payout, tax-free uplift)
scenarios.gate: Client has met a disability/permanent-incapacity condition of release; super boosted by a TPD/disability insurance payout
scenarios.figures: Staged one-off withdrawal amounts; tax-free vs taxable %; 22% tax withheld
scenarios.strat: We recommend you make one-off lump sum withdrawals from your new Accumulation fund as a disability super benefit (e.g. $80,550 in FY25/26, $40,000 in FY26/27, $15,000 in FY27/28) to fund your planned expenses, alongside commencing a pension income to cover your cashflow shortfall.
scenarios.outcome: At the time of writing, it is estimated that your balance after uplift will comprise approximately 48% tax-free and 52% taxable components.
why: Because you have met a permanent-incapacity condition of release, you can access your superannuation as a disability super benefit, which receives a tax-free component uplift (the tax-free proportion is increased to reflect your prospective service period to retirement).
Staged lump-sum withdrawals fund known upcoming expenses while keeping the balance invested in line with your risk profile.
risks: The 22% tax will be withheld at the time of each withdrawal. You are likely to receive a refund for the excess tax withheld when you lodge your tax return — consult an accountant before implementing.

As these withdrawals are intended for immediate expenses, no adverse impact on your Disability Support Pension (DSP) is expected under the assets and income test. However, if the withdrawn funds are not spent and remain in your savings account, your DSP payments may temporarily reduce until your balance falls below the relevant threshold.
The projection does not account for additional ad hoc withdrawals or material increases in pension drawdowns; we review annually.
alts: Draw all income via pension only — discounted as it does not provide the lump sums needed for your planned one-off expenses.

scenarios.name: Reversionary beneficiary nomination (pension phase)
scenarios.strat: We recommend you nominate a reversionary beneficiary within your recommended pension funds. A reversionary nomination allows the nominated dependant to automatically receive the pension payments in the event of your passing.
scenarios.outcome: Seamless continuation of pension income to your surviving spouse, avoiding a lump-sum death benefit and probate delay.
why: The pension automatically continues to your nominated dependant on death, preserving the tax-effective income stream.
Death benefit payment option — you can nominate dependants under the non-lapsing binding election, or you can select an automatic reversionary pension under the pension plan.
risks: A reversionary nomination is generally only available to a spouse/de facto; it reduces flexibility if the beneficiary's circumstances change (a new nomination is required).
If the reversionary beneficiary pre-deceases you, the benefit reverts to your estate unless a backup nomination is in place.
alts: Non-lapsing binding death benefit nomination only — provides a lump sum rather than a continuing income stream; less seamless for a surviving spouse in pension phase.

scenarios.name: Seamless accumulation-to-pension transfer (no asset sale; avoid CGT / poor-timing sale)
scenarios.gate: Commencing an account-based pension from an existing accumulation account on the same platform
scenarios.strat: We recommend a seamless transfer from accumulation to pension — you are not required to sell down your assets to transfer into the pension phase.
scenarios.outcome: Your assets move into the tax-free pension environment without being sold, preserving your position.
why: This can prevent unnecessary Capital Gains Tax consequences and/or sale of assets at a time of unfavourable market conditions.
It maintains your existing investment holdings and their long-term timing.
risks: Some platforms charge for in-specie transfers; holdings remain subject to market movements in the pension phase.
alts: Sell down in accumulation and re-buy in pension — discounted as it can crystallise CGT and forces a sale that may occur at an unfavourable time.

scenarios.name: In-specie transfer of super on separation (SMSF asset split to personal super)
scenarios.gate: Separation with an SMSF or jointly-held super to be split
scenarios.strat: Following your recent separation, we recommend completing an in-specie transfer of your allocated SMSF assets (e.g. the platform investment and cash account) into a personal superannuation fund tailored to your needs.
scenarios.outcome: Your share of the fund moves to a personal super account without selling the underlying assets.
why: An in-specie transfer preserves your portfolio and avoids crystallising capital gains, buy/sell spreads and market-timing risk that a sell-down would create.
risks: There may be transaction costs involved in establishing the strategy.
In-specie transfer may not be available for all asset types; the asset split documentation must be finalised before execution.
alts: Sell the SMSF assets and roll cash to personal super — discounted as it crystallises CGT and transaction costs.

scenarios.name: Commence pension before rebalancing to minimise CGT (defer rebalance to pension phase)
scenarios.gate: SMSF/super moving to pension phase with a portfolio rebalance required
scenarios.strat: We recommend commencing pension phase prior to the rebalance, and deferring the rebalance of the portfolio until pension phase commences, to reduce the CGT impact on the portion of the balance transferred to retirement phase. Please consult your accountant to confirm the tax implications.
scenarios.outcome: Assets are rebalanced once in the tax-free pension environment, reducing the capital gains tax on the changeover.
why: Selling to rebalance in accumulation phase can trigger CGT at 10–15%; deferring the rebalance until the assets support a retirement-phase income stream reduces or removes that tax.
Where the rebalance is done within the Account-Based Pension accounts, we do not anticipate it will crystallise a capital gain, so you should not incur CGT as a result of the rebalance.
On platforms that match buy and sell orders internally, the rebalance offsets purchases and sales and keeps your portfolio fully invested, avoiding time-out-of-market risk.

Where an SMSF asset (e.g. an investment property) is to be sold, commencing the Account-Based Pension before the sale means the fund is in retirement phase, so the sale is not expected to be subject to capital gains tax. Please consult your accountant to confirm prior to implementing.
risks: Markets may move while the rebalance is deferred; timing should be confirmed with your accountant.
alts: Rebalance immediately in accumulation phase — discounted as it crystallises avoidable CGT.

scenarios.name: Retain an existing SMSF (operate, add account, redirect contributions, reinvest)
scenarios.gate: Existing SMSF that is to be kept (not wound up)
scenarios.strat: We recommend you retain your existing SMSF. We recommend you establish a new investment account held by the SMSF (invested in line with your risk profile), retain your existing SMSF cash account, provide your employer with the fund details so future contributions are directed to the SMSF, and reinvest distributions from the SMSF investment portfolio.
scenarios.outcome: Your SMSF continues as your super vehicle, with a customised investment account, a central cash account for transactions and compliance costs, all contributions consolidated to the fund, and distributions reinvested to compound.
why: Retaining the SMSF cash account consolidates all super transactions into one central account, easing monitoring and providing liquidity for ongoing costs and administrative fees of being an SMSF trustee.
Directing all future employer (and personal) contributions to the SMSF consolidates your super into one fund for easier management.
Reinvesting distributions accelerates growth potential through compounding.
risks: As trustee you remain responsible for the fund's compliance, administration and costs.
Reinvesting distributions means no access to that income until a condition of release is met.
alts: Wind up the SMSF and roll to a retail/platform fund — discounted where the SMSF holds assets (e.g. an investment property) central to your long-term strategy.

scenarios.name: SMSF with corporate trustee holding a geared investment property (LRBA cashflow)
scenarios.gate: SMSF holding (or acquiring) real property, typically with secured debt
scenarios.strat: Your SMSF (corporate trustee — Pty Ltd ATF the fund) holds an investment property with secured debt. We recommend consolidating both members' existing super into the SMSF via full rollover, maintaining a dedicated cash reserve for SMSF administration and property-related costs, and deploying the property's net rental income to fund your ongoing regular SMSF contributions.
scenarios.outcome: Both members' super is pooled in the SMSF behind the property, with a cash buffer for costs and rental surplus recycled into ongoing contributions.
why: A corporate trustee structure (Pty Ltd as trustee for the fund) simplifies succession and limits trustee liability compared with individual trustees.
Consolidating both members' balances and the rental surplus into the fund concentrates capital behind the long-term property strategy.
risks: SMSF borrowing and property holding add audit, compliance and liquidity complexity; the fund must hold enough cash to meet loan repayments and costs.
Property is illiquid and concentrated; a fall in value or rental income affects the fund's ability to meet obligations.
alts: Wind up the SMSF — discounted as the fund was established to hold the investment property as part of your long-term superannuation strategy.

scenarios.name: SMSF wind-up / consolidation to a retail fund (non-separation, cost/suitability driven)
scenarios.gate: Existing SMSF whose original purpose no longer applies / costs outweigh benefit
scenarios.figures: Estimated reduction in ongoing admin fees p.a.
scenarios.strat: You have asked us to review the long-term suitability of retaining your SMSF. The initial purpose of establishing the SMSF was to purchase a property; as that is no longer being pursued, we recommend you close your SMSF and rollover the full benefits to a new retail/platform fund customised for your needs.
scenarios.outcome: Your super is simplified into a retail/platform fund, removing the cost and trustee responsibilities of the SMSF while keeping access to the recommended investment portfolio.
why: We believe an SMSF is not the right vehicle for your super, considering your current SMSF position.
By simplifying your superannuation you will not be burdened by the responsibilities of operating an SMSF.
Since you are not actively considering purchasing property through your superannuation as initially planned, closing the SMSF aligns better with your current goals and objectives.
Transferring from an SMSF to a retail superannuation fund reduces your ongoing administrative fees and eliminates your legal and administrative responsibilities as an SMSF trustee.
We have discussed the short and long-term implications, including the costs that would occur if you ever wished to re-establish the SMSF in the future after winding it up now.
risks: The SMSF wind-up will require the sale of the existing share portfolio within the fund, which may have capital gains implications and transaction costs.
Wind-up costs include completion of the current and previous SMSF financial statements, tax returns and any audit/compliance costs.
alts: Retain your existing SMSF — discounted as an SMSF has high costs and ongoing legal/administrative trustee requirements that are not needed to meet your retirement goals where the original purpose is no longer being pursued.

scenarios.name: Establish new fund + partial rollover, retain minimum for higher SG contributions
scenarios.strat: We recommend you retain the minimum balance in your existing fund to keep receiving your higher employer SG contributions, and roll the remainder to the new recommended fund.
why: Some employers pay a higher SG into the existing fund; retaining a minimum balance preserves that benefit while still consolidating the bulk of your super.
risks: Two accounts mean two sets of fees until the arrangement ends.

scenarios.name: Commence an Account-Based Pension and draw an income (minimum % or set amount)
scenarios.strat: We recommend you commence an Account-Based Pension and draw [the minimum % / $___ p.a.] to meet your income needs / top up your pension / fund your financial-freedom goal.
why: Pension-phase earnings are tax-free and the income stream funds your retirement spending.
risks: Minimum drawdowns are mandatory and apply even in a market downturn.

scenarios.name: CGT implications on a super changeover (SMSF, or rebalance Vanguard↔CARE) (free text)
scenarios.strat: [Free-type the CGT implications of the super changeover — applies for SMSF or a rebalance between Vanguard and CARE; not required for a standard rollover. Consult accountant.]

scenarios.name: Phase a lump-sum super investment via money-on-the-move (DCA the rollover)
scenarios.strat: For the lump sum entering super, we recommend phasing it into the market via the money-on-the-move framework — bringing forward instalments as markets fall.
why: Phasing a large rollover smooths your entry price and reduces timing risk.

areas.name: 6 · Superannuation Contributions
areas.note: Salary sacrifice / carry‑forward wording is verbatim. The remaining contribution types are drafts for your review.

scenarios.name: Salary sacrifice / concessional contributions
scenarios.strat: We recommend you [continue / increase / decrease / cease] your salary sacrifice (concessional) contributions of $___.
scenarios.outcome: Making concessional contributions builds your retirement savings tax‑effectively and provides net tax savings of approximately $XXX p.a.
why: Save on income tax because your salary contributed into super is taxed at 15% (up to your concessional contributions cap), not your marginal tax rate, regardless of how much you earn.
Boost your super by contributing more now, creating a bigger nest egg for your retirement.

Suitable if you are under 75 and eligible to contribute, have a marginal tax rate above 15%, and can sacrifice income without a large impact on your lifestyle, with an employer willing to offer the arrangement.
Concessional contributions are taxed at 15% within super (up to your cap), not your marginal tax rate.
risks: Care should be taken to ensure your employee entitlements are not adversely impacted as a result of salary sacrificing, or that you don't breach your concessional contributions cap. Contributions are preserved until a condition of release is met.
alts: Invest the surplus outside super instead — discounted where the tax‑effectiveness of concessional contributions better meets the goal, noting reduced accessibility.

scenarios.name: Carry-forward (catch-up) concessional contributions
scenarios.strat: We recommend you make a carry-forward concessional contribution of $XXX, utilising your unused concessional cap amounts from previous years (after the 15% contributions tax).
scenarios.outcome: Using your carry‑forward concessional cap allows a larger tax‑deductible contribution this year, reducing your assessable income.
why: The carry-forward arrangements involve accessing unused concessional cap amounts from previous years. An unused cap amount occurs when the concessional contributions you made in a financial year were less than your general concessional contributions cap. You can use caps from up to five previous financial years.
Tax-effective: contributions are taxed at 15% rather than your marginal rate.
risks: To use your unused cap amounts: your total super balance at the end of 30 June of the previous financial year must be less than $500,000, and you must have made concessional contributions in the year that exceeded your general cap. Contributions are preserved until a condition of release is met.
alts: Contribute only up to the standard cap — discounted where the carry‑forward provides a greater tax benefit this year.

scenarios.name: Non-concessional contribution
scenarios.strat: This financial year, we recommend withdrawing [$amount] from your existing pension account and re-contributing it as a once-off non-concessional contribution as part of a re-contribution strategy. Next financial year, we recommend utilising the bring-forward rule to make a further non-concessional contribution of up to [$cap].
scenarios.outcome: Increasing the tax-free proportion of your superannuation reduces potential tax payable on death benefits, particularly for non-tax-dependant beneficiaries such as your adult children.
why: Your existing pension comprises a taxable and a tax-free component. Withdrawing funds and re-contributing them as non-concessional contributions increases the tax-free proportion of your superannuation over time and improves overall tax efficiency.
It is expected to reduce potential tax payable on death benefits, particularly for non-tax-dependant beneficiaries such as adult children.
The strategy allows for optimal use of your available non-concessional contribution caps, including the bring-forward rule, to enhance long-term outcomes.
risks: There is a risk that you don't follow or stick with the strategy, particularly at market extremes.
If you don't communicate changes in your circumstances, goals and objectives to us, your portfolio may no longer be appropriate.
The underlying investments within super are invested in investment funds. This involves some investment risk and does not guarantee your returns — values may fall from time to time.
alts: Retain your existing pension account with current funds allocation. I discounted this strategy as the existing account has a high taxable component which makes your super less tax-effective as a wealth-transfer tool — compared to the tax-free component, it creates a larger tax liability for beneficiaries.

scenarios.name: Bring-forward non-concessional contribution
scenarios.strat: We recommend you use the bring-forward rule to make a non-concessional contribution of $XXX (bringing forward up to three years of your non-concessional cap).
scenarios.outcome: The bring‑forward rule lets you contribute a larger after‑tax amount now, accelerating your retirement savings.
why: The non-concessional cap is $120,000 for 2024/2025. If you are under 75 years of age during the financial year, a $360,000 contribution can be made by 'bringing forward' two years' worth of contribution caps (in addition to contributions from that year). Accelerates the build-up of retirement savings in the low-tax super environment.

The bring-forward non-concessional contribution can be funded from the proceeds of a property sale (e.g. $360,000 using a portion of the proceeds), moving sale proceeds into the tax-free/low-tax super environment across the three-year window.

The bring-forward rule lets you use future years' non-concessional caps to make a larger one-off contribution now, maximising the funds in the tax-free super environment to draw retirement income from.

The contribution can be made via in-specie transfer of an existing investment portfolio (rather than selling to cash and re-buying), saving transaction costs and buy/sell spreads and avoiding time out of the market — noting the in-specie transfer crystallises CGT on the transferred assets.
risks: Eligibility depends on your age and total super balance at the prior 30 June; contributions in excess of applicable limits will attract penalty tax. Triggering the bring-forward restricts contributions in the following years; contributions are preserved.
Sale proceeds must be held in cash until the contribution is made, which may mean time out of the market.
alts: Contribute within the standard annual cap — discounted where the larger up‑front contribution better meets the goal.

scenarios.name: Spouse contribution
scenarios.strat: [Name], we recommend you make an after-tax spouse contribution of up to $3,000 p.a. to [Spouse]'s super to boost their retirement savings and receive a tax offset.
scenarios.outcome: A spouse contribution boosts your spouse's retirement savings and may provide you with a tax offset.
why: Under current 2025/26 rules, you may claim an 18% tax offset on spouse super contributions up to $3,000, for a maximum offset of $540 where your spouse's income is $37,000 or less (reducing to nil at $40,000).

Because spouse contributions are from after-tax money, they aren't subject to the 15% contributions tax and are tax-free on withdrawal. Boosts the super of a lower-income/non-working spouse and helps you grow retirement savings as a couple.
risks: Contributions count toward your spouse's non-concessional cap; both must be Australian residents and not living separately and apart on a permanent basis; your spouse must be under 75.
alts: Contribute to your own super instead — discounted where equalising balances or the spouse offset better meets the goal.

scenarios.name: Government co-contribution
scenarios.strat: We recommend you make a non-concessional (after-tax) contribution of up to $1,000 to superannuation to take advantage of the Federal Government co-contribution scheme.
scenarios.outcome: A small after‑tax contribution can attract up to $500 from the Government, an immediate uplift to your super.
why: You receive a tax-free super contribution from the federal government when you make a non-concessional contribution to your super account, subject to satisfying a work test, an income test and an age test.
If you earn $47,488 or less (for the 2025/2026 year), the government pays $0.50 for every dollar you contribute in after-tax dollars, up to a maximum of $500 a year (reducing to nil at $62,488).
risks: Eligibility depends on your income, age and total super balance; the contribution is preserved.
alts: Do not contribute — discounted as it forgoes the Government co‑contribution where you are eligible.

scenarios.name: Contribution splitting
scenarios.strat: [Name], we recommend you split up to 85% of your concessional (employer and personal tax-deductible) contributions of $XXX to [Spouse]'s super account.
scenarios.outcome: Contribution splitting equalises your balances and can provide earlier access to super and a reduced tax liability.
why: Super contributions splitting generally allows you to split up to 85% of your employer super contributions and personal tax-deductible (concessional) contributions to your spouse's super account, so you can both maximise the benefits of super.
Splitting contributions to a spouse who will reach age 60 before you may allow you earlier access to your super monies and the tax-free status of super withdrawals for those aged 60 or over.
Suitable if you have a spouse eligible to receive super contributions, a spouse who will reach 60 before you, or you want to boost your spouse's super savings.
risks: Not all super funds offer contribution splitting. Super is subject to preservation rules and contributions cannot be accessed until a condition of release is met. When split to your spouse's account they do not count towards your spouse's concessional contributions cap (they count against yours).
alts: Retain the contributions in your own account — discounted where balance equalisation better meets the goal.

scenarios.name: Personal deductible contribution
triggers: claim a tax deduction for contribution
scenarios.strat: We recommend you commence making yearly concessional (personal deductible) contributions, setting aside the funds in your cash account through the year and making the contribution as a lump sum each year, then claiming a tax deduction for it.
scenarios.outcome: You use your concessional cap via a personal deductible contribution, reducing taxable income and building super, without needing a salary-sacrifice arrangement with your employer.
why: Making ongoing concessional contributions helps reduce the effect of adviser fees and insurance premiums on your superannuation balance.
Claiming the contribution as a tax deduction provides net tax savings by moving income into the 15% super environment instead of your marginal rate.
risks: You must stay within the concessional cap to avoid excess-contribution tax, and lodge a valid notice of intent to claim the deduction with your fund.
alts: Salary sacrifice via your employer — equivalent outcome but requires an employer arrangement; non-concessional contribution — discounted as it gives no deduction.

scenarios.name: Work test note (age 67+)
scenarios.strat: We recommend ensuring contributions are made prior to turning age 67, due to potential work test requirements and contribution eligibility restrictions.
why: Prior to age 67, a person can make superannuation contributions without restriction. Between 67 and 74, tax deduction claims can only be made if the work test is satisfied (gainfully employed at least 40 hours over not more than 30 consecutive days in the financial year).

scenarios.name: Downsizer contribution
scenarios.strat: We recommend you utilise the downsizer contribution strategy to make a one-off contribution of up to $300,000 each ($600,000 per couple) to your new superannuation account from the proceeds of the sale of your home.
scenarios.outcome: The proceeds of your home sale are moved into the concessionally-taxed superannuation environment and used to fund a tax-free retirement income stream.
why: The downsizer contribution lets you move up to $300,000 each from the sale of a main residence (owned 10+ years, age 55+) into super, regardless of your other contribution caps or total super balance.
It allows the proceeds to be professionally managed in line with your risk profile and drawn as tax-free retirement income.
risks: There is the normal risk of markets falling and unforeseen circumstances requiring you to draw funds when markets are down.

By investing your cash into a superannuation fund instead of a bank account you lose capital stability and a known rate of return. You also lose access to the government guarantee on deposits up to $250,000.
Funds are preserved — you cannot access them until you meet a condition of release.
alts: Retain the proceeds in cash/term deposits — discounted as it forgoes the tax-effective superannuation environment and professional management.
Contribute via non-concessional contributions instead — discounted where the downsizer rules allow a larger contribution without using your NCC caps.

scenarios.name: Contributions reserving strategy (double concessional cap before age 67)
scenarios.gate: Super contributions scoped; client under 67 with capacity
scenarios.strat: We recommend implementing a contributions reserving strategy within your SMSF by making concessional contributions totalling [2 × cap] prior to 30 June. The full amount will be contributed and claimed as a tax deduction, with [one cap] in the current financial year and [one cap] in July (next financial year). This allows use of both years' concessional caps before age 67, when work test rules may limit further contributions.
scenarios.outcome: You bring forward and claim two years' worth of concessional caps in the current financial year, maximising the tax deduction and capital moved into super before the work test applies.
why: By maximising your concessional contribution caps across both financial years before age 67, you enhance tax efficiency by reducing personal taxable income and increasing capital within the superannuation environment before work test requirements may apply.
risks: The strategy relies on your accountant confirming eligibility and lodging the relevant ATO contribution-reserving forms; incorrect implementation can cause an excess concessional contribution.
The Fund must hold the reserved contribution and allocate it within the prescribed period.
alts: Make a single year's concessional contribution only — discounted as it forgoes the additional cap available before the work test applies.

scenarios.name: First Home Super Saver Scheme (FHSSS)
scenarios.gate: Client(s) saving for a first home; eligible to make voluntary contributions
scenarios.figures: Voluntary contributions up to the FHSSS limit; salary-sacrifice amount
scenarios.strat: We recommend you each utilise the First Home Super Saver Scheme (FHSSS) to assist with the purchase of your first property: make a lump-sum personal contribution before 30 June, commence salary sacrificing up to the annual limit, and continue making voluntary contributions each year. Once you are prepared to purchase, withdraw your voluntary contributions and associated earnings by requesting a determination through myGov followed by a release request.
scenarios.outcome: You save for your deposit inside super at concessional tax rates, then release the funds (plus deemed earnings) to put toward your first home.
why: Voluntary contributions are taxed concessionally in super, and the released amount (including associated earnings) is taxed more favourably than ordinary income, helping you build your deposit faster.
risks: Funds are accessible only for an eligible first-home purchase; if you don't proceed, the contributions remain preserved in super.
Income/timing matters — salary sacrifice may interact with co-contribution eligibility, and the release requires a myGov determination then a release request.
alts: Save the deposit outside super — discounted as it forgoes the FHSSS tax concession.

scenarios.name: Salary packaging (employer-provided, e.g. health / PBI sector)
scenarios.gate: Employer offers salary packaging (commonly health/charity/PBI employers)
scenarios.figures: Maximum annual packaging amount available from the employer
scenarios.strat: We recommend you commence salary packaging your income to the maximum amount available to you (e.g. $9,010 p.a.).
scenarios.outcome: Pre-tax income is diverted to packaged benefits, reducing your taxable income.
why: Salary packaging reduces your assessable income at your marginal tax rate without using your concessional contribution cap, improving your after-tax position.
risks: Availability depends on your employer and role; it ceases if you change employers.
It can interact with means-tested benefits; coordinate with any salary sacrifice so you do not exceed your concessional cap.
alts: Forgo packaging and use post-tax income — discounted as it forgoes the tax saving available through your employer.

scenarios.name: Carry-forward concessional contribution to offset CGT on an asset sale
scenarios.gate: A capital gain is being realised (e.g. investment property sale) and unused concessional cap is available
scenarios.figures: Estimated capital gain; carry-forward concessional contribution; CGT before vs after
scenarios.strat: We recommend you each make a once-off concessional contribution using the carry-forward rule in the year you realise the capital gain (e.g. $26,000 each), claiming it as a tax deduction to reduce your assessable capital gain.
scenarios.outcome: The deduction reduces the tax payable on the sale (e.g. reducing the CGT liability from $41,000 to $33,000) while boosting your super.
why: Unused concessional cap from prior years can be 'carried forward' and used in a high-income year to shelter a capital gain, moving money into the concessionally-taxed super environment.
risks: Requires sufficient carry-forward cap room and a total super balance under the threshold; the contribution must be made in the same financial year as the gain.
Contributions are preserved until a condition of release is met.
alts: Invest the sale proceeds outside super — discounted as it forgoes the CGT-offset benefit; or use the non-concessional cap (no deduction).

scenarios.name: Notice of intent — claim a tax deduction on unclaimed personal contributions
scenarios.strat: We recommend you submit a notice of intent to claim a tax deduction on any unclaimed personal contributions made this and the previous financial year.
why: Claiming the deduction converts after-tax contributions into concessional ones, reducing your taxable income.

scenarios.name: Arrange salary sacrifice with employer (switch post-tax to pre-tax)
scenarios.strat: We recommend you speak with your employer to switch your current post-tax contributions to pre-tax salary-sacrifice contributions.
why: Pre-tax (salary-sacrifice) contributions are taxed at 15% rather than your marginal rate.

scenarios.name: Division 293 tax note (high-income earners)
scenarios.strat: Note: as a higher-income earner you may be subject to Division 293 tax — an additional 15% on concessional contributions where your income plus contributions exceeds the threshold.

scenarios.name: Division 296 tax note (total super balance over $3m)
scenarios.strat: Note: Division 296 may apply an additional tax on earnings attributable to the portion of your total super balance above $3m.

areas.name: 7 · Personal Protection
areas.note: New, top‑up, replace/takeover and retain wording is verbatim from your SOAs (Linked/Own‑Occupation, inside‑super vs personal, 90‑day wait, etc.).

scenarios.name: Levels of cover as per quotes
triggers: levels of cover as per quotes
scenarios.strat: Levels of cover as per the attached quotes.

scenarios.name: Take out new cover (Life / TPD / Trauma / IP)
scenarios.strat:
We recommend you take out new insurance cover through [Insurer] and therefore be insured for the following amounts:
• Life $XXX (Linked)
• TPD $XXX (Linked & Own-Occupation)
• Trauma $XXX
• IP $XXX per month (Indemnity, 90 day wait, to age 65)
We recommend a Variable Age-Stepped premium structure for all cover.
We strongly recommend you apply for the recommended cover and do not cancel any existing cover until the new cover is in force.
scenarios.outcome: You will have affordable cover that meets your needs, including covering your debts, with appropriate features and benefits to maintain your family and lifestyle.
why: Your full existing personal debt, partial existing/proposed investment debt, and any funeral and final expenses will be covered. A lump sum has been added to gross up the life cover to allow linking with TPD and Trauma benefits, reducing the overall cost compared with holding standalone TPD and Trauma cover.
The lump sum for investment will cover $XXX per annum income in perpetuity, calculated on an assumed income return of 5% and no capital drawdown.
We have recommended TPD with Own Occupation which is the highest level of cover and ensures you are covered if you are unable to return to the occupation you were last engaged.

We have recommended income protection covering up to 70% of your income and super, with a 90 day wait (you have available cash and leave to fund this period, reducing cost) and the longest benefit period to ensure maximum coverage across your working life.
risks: If personal insurance cover is held in a superannuation environment, any claim for the insured benefit is subject to superannuation release laws, so assessment can take some time, and proceeds may be subject to tax.
Some Crisis Recovery conditions will not be covered during the first 90 days of a new policy (this does not generally apply when replacing like cover).
The premium quoted is a guide only; 'loading' of premiums can occur following full underwriting.
Funding insurance premiums from your superannuation will have an impact on your retirement balance, estimated at $XXX or XX% over a 5 year period.
alts: Apply for cover with a lower sum insured — discounted as it does not provide adequate protection in the event of a long-term illness/injury or death.
Apply for Standalone TPD — discounted as you are happy for TPD to be linked with Life due to premium affordability.
Apply for Income Protection with a shorter benefit period (e.g. 2 or 5 years) — discounted as it does not provide adequate protection.
Apply for Income Protection with a longer waiting period (e.g. 6/12 months) — discounted as you may not have sufficient funds to support you during the waiting period.
Self-insure using your net worth — discounted as your need for insurance exceeds the value of your net worth and you are not comfortable with the inherent level of risk.

scenarios.name: Top-up / increase existing cover
scenarios.strat: We recommend you top-up your insurance cover through [Insurer] and therefore be insured for the following amounts: [amounts]. We recommend you apply for your top-up insurance cover through [Insurer].
scenarios.outcome: You will have affordable additional cover that meets your needs, including covering your debts, with appropriate features and benefits to maintain your family and lifestyle.
why: Your full existing personal debt, partial existing/proposed investment debt, and any funeral and final expenses will be covered.
A lump sum has been added to gross up the life cover to allow linking with TPD and Trauma benefits, reducing the overall cost compared with standalone cover.
risks: Your total premiums will increase, however the recommended policies provide for an increase to appropriate sums insured.
Funding insurance premiums from your superannuation will have an impact on your retirement balance estimated at $XXX or XX% over a 5 year period.
alts: (uses the standard insurance alternatives above)

scenarios.name: Replace / cancel & take out new cover (with takeover terms)
scenarios.strat: [Name], we recommend you cancel your existing insurance and take out new insurance cover and therefore be insured for the following amounts: [amounts]. [Name], we strongly recommend that you apply for the recommended replacement cover and do not cancel your current insurance within [Fund] until the new insurances are in force. This will ensure that if your application is declined for any reason you will still have some insurance in place.
scenarios.outcome: Once the recommended insurances are in place, cancelling your existing cover consolidates your insurance with one provider, easing administration and avoiding multiple policy fees.
why: The recommended replacement cover provides additional benefits (such as improved definitions and access to trauma insurance) compared to your existing cover.
Your recommended insurance will be underwritten, which means come claim time you know where you stand with a payout; your current cover has never been underwritten, which leaves uncertainty.
Holding consolidated insurance with one provider eases ongoing administration and prevents paying multiple policy fees.
risks: In replacing insurance policies, no two policies are exactly identical — depending on the claim circumstances one policy may provide a better benefit than another. We do not believe there are any significant disadvantages to our recommendation.
There may be restrictions in the new policy or the cover may be accepted on different terms than the existing policy.
You lose any cover you currently hold as soon as it is cancelled — wait to cancel until you receive confirmation from the new insurer.

Suicide (temporary) — as the new policy replaces part of your current cover, you will lose cover in the event of suicide during the first 13 months of the new life cover; this is reinstated once the policy has been in force more than 13 months.
alts: Rollover part of your super in order to retain your existing insurance cover within super — discounted as the recommended replacement provides additional benefits, and a partial rollover would leave more than one super account to track.

scenarios.name: Retain existing cover (inside super)
scenarios.strat: We recommend you retain your existing insurance through [Fund] and remain insured for the following amounts: [amounts]. (Where applicable: [Name], we recommend you retain your existing Life insurance while cancelling your TPD and IP insurances through [Fund].)
scenarios.outcome: Retaining your existing cover maintains your underwritten terms while keeping premiums funded from super to protect your cashflow.
why: Retains your underwritten Life & TPD insurance.
By holding insurance cover inside superannuation, the cost of the premiums can be met from your superannuation balance, which frees up your cashflow for other purposes.
As much cover as possible is held within the superannuation environment to reduce the effect on your personal cashflow.
risks: If personal insurance cover is held in a superannuation environment, any claim is subject to superannuation release laws (assessment can take time) and proceeds may be subject to tax.
The premium quoted is a guide only; loading can occur following full underwriting.
alts: Apply for cover completely outside superannuation — discounted as the premium cost would then need to be met from your everyday income.
Self-insure using your net worth — discounted as your need for insurance exceeds your net worth.

scenarios.name: Income Protection — retain existing
scenarios.strat: We have recommended retaining your income protection policy with 75% of your income and super. We have recommended retaining the 13 week wait period as you have available cash and leave to fund 13 weeks of expenses (this reduces the overall cost), and retaining the longest benefit period to ensure maximum coverage across your working life.
scenarios.outcome: Retaining your income protection maintains your income replacement while keeping the cost efficient.
why: Maintains income replacement to age 65/longest benefit period, ensuring you can afford everyday expenses if unable to work.
risks: Income protection does not fully replace your income (generally not designed to cover 100%), which may create a shortfall in disposable income.
Indemnity cover is subject to assessment of your income prior to claim — if your income has decreased you may receive a lower payout.
alts: Apply for IP with a longer waiting period — discounted as you may not have sufficient funds during the waiting period.

scenarios.name: Employer-paid / default cover (retain or note)
scenarios.strat: We recommend you retain your existing employer-paid (default) insurance cover of [amounts] held within [Fund], in addition to the recommended cover. (Or, where being replaced: we recommend you cancel your default cover within [Fund] once the new underwritten cover is in force.)
scenarios.outcome: Retaining your employer-paid cover maintains valuable cover at no cost to your cashflow while the recommended underwritten cover provides certainty at claim time.
why: Default cover is provided at no direct cost to you (premiums met by your employer / within the fund) and is generally provided on an automatic-acceptance basis without underwriting.
Retaining it provides an additional layer of cover alongside the recommended underwritten policy.
risks: Default/group cover is not underwritten, so at claim time the insurer may assess pre-existing conditions and exclusions, creating uncertainty. Cover usually ceases if you change employer or your account becomes inactive.
Default cover levels are generic and may not match your actual needs.
alts: Cancel the default cover and rely solely on the new underwritten cover — discounted where the default cover provides valuable additional cover at no cashflow cost.

scenarios.name: Apply for child cover
scenarios.strat: We recommend you take out Child Cover of $XXX for [child/children] under your policy.
scenarios.outcome: Child Cover provides a lump sum to support your family if a child suffers a defined trauma event, and can later convert to adult cover.
why: Provides a lump sum on a child's defined trauma event to fund medical costs and time away from work.
If the insured child meets the eligibility criteria, they may convert the Child Cover to an equivalent adult Life Insurance Plan without reapplying or providing medical evidence.
risks: Child Cover is limited to defined conditions; some conditions carry a qualifying period.
Premiums add to the overall policy cost.
alts: Self-fund a child's medical/recovery costs — discounted where a lump sum provides more certainty.

scenarios.name: Premium structure — stepped vs level / variable age-stepped
scenarios.strat: We recommend a Variable Age-Stepped premium structure for all cover. [Couple variant: where a client prefers long-term affordability, recommend a level premium structure for that person, and a variable age-stepped structure for the other.]
scenarios.outcome: Your premium structure is matched to your affordability preference — variable age-stepped for immediate affordability and flexibility, level for long-term affordability.
why: We have recommended a Variable Age-Stepped premium structure which will give you immediate affordability and ongoing flexibility of your coverage.
[Level variant] We have recommended retaining a level premium structure which will give you long-term affordability.
risks: Premiums increase over time (for stepped / variable age-stepped structures).
Holding cover inside super reduces your retirement balance over time.
Underwriting may apply medical exclusions or loadings (e.g. higher premiums for smoker status); a suicide exclusion typically applies for the first 13 months.
alts: Structure all premiums as level. While this would reduce your ongoing premium payable, I have discounted this strategy as premiums would be significantly higher initially making short-term affordability an issue. The recommended insurance structure provides immediate affordability and flexibility in the sum insured.

scenarios.name: Cancel cover no longer required
scenarios.strat: We recommend you cancel your existing [cover type] of $XXX as it exceeds your current insurance needs.
scenarios.outcome: Cancelling cover you no longer need removes an unnecessary premium cost, improving your cashflow.
why: Reduces premium outlay where your need for cover has reduced (e.g. debts repaid, assets accumulated, children independent).
risks: Once cancelled you lose the cover immediately; if your circumstances change, new cover would require fresh underwriting and may be more expensive or declined. Do not cancel existing cover until you are certain it is no longer required.
alts: Retain the cover — discounted where it clearly exceeds your assessed need and the premium is better directed elsewhere.

scenarios.name: Income Protection — increasing/CPI-indexed claim benefit
scenarios.strat: We recommend an increasing-claim option so that, while you are receiving payments, your benefit is indexed at each review date in line with CPI. This increase is capped to 5% if income protection is structured through superannuation.
scenarios.outcome: Your income protection payments keep pace with inflation during a long claim.
why: The increasing-claim option protects the real value of your benefit payments over a multi-year claim.
risks: The 5% cap (for super-held cover) may not fully match CPI in high-inflation periods; the indexed benefit increases your premium; indexation applies only while you are on claim.
alts: Level (non-indexed) benefit — lower ongoing premium but the benefit's real value erodes during a long claim.

scenarios.name: Trauma cover with reinstatement benefit
scenarios.strat: We have recommended a trauma reinstatement benefit which allows you to reinstate the trauma benefit after a claim has been paid.
scenarios.outcome: After a trauma claim is paid, your cover can be reinstated so you remain protected against a later, unrelated trauma event.
why: Recovery from one condition does not remove the risk of a later, unrelated trauma event; reinstatement restores cover for that scenario.
risks: The reinstated benefit may be subject to conditions/waiting periods and adds to the premium; not all insurers offer it.
alts: Single-claim trauma cover only — lower cost but no protection against a subsequent event.

scenarios.name: Linked cover with buy-back feature
scenarios.strat: As your TPD/Trauma cover is linked to your Life/TPD cover, a claim on one type of cover will reduce the sum insured on the other — we recommend adding the cover buy-back feature so the reduced cover can be reinstated after a claim.
scenarios.outcome: After a linked claim reduces your other cover, the buy-back feature restores it without re-underwriting.
why: Linked cover is more cost-effective than standalone policies, and the buy-back feature removes the main drawback by restoring the reduced cover after a claim.
risks: The buy-back feature adds to the premium; it applies within defined terms and age limits.
alts: Standalone (unlinked) policies — no claim-driven reduction but materially higher premiums; or linked cover without buy-back (cheaper, but cover reduces after a claim).

scenarios.name: Future insurability / guaranteed future increases
scenarios.strat: Your recommended policies contain future insurability clauses, meaning that if your circumstances change in future you can increase your cover periodically without further medical underwriting.
scenarios.outcome: You can raise your cover at set life events or intervals without a new health assessment.
why: This locks in your current health rating, so deterioration in your health does not block reasonable future increases within policy limits.
risks: Increases are limited to set amounts/intervals and have age limits; the increased benefit is still subject to claims assessment.
alts: Lock cover at today's level with no increase option — lower flexibility if your needs grow.

scenarios.name: Own-occupation TPD definition
scenarios.gate: TPD cover recommended for a specialised/high-income occupation
scenarios.strat: We have recommended TPD with an 'Own Occupation' definition, which is the highest level of cover.
scenarios.outcome: A claim can be met if you are unable to work in your own specific occupation, rather than any occupation.
why: Own-occupation cover suits a specialised or high-income role where being unable to perform that specific occupation, even if able to do another, would end your earning capacity.
risks: Own-occupation cover costs more than any-occupation; where linked, a claim reduces the linked cover unless a buy-back feature is added.
alts: Any-occupation TPD — cheaper but a narrower claim trigger (must be unable to work in any occupation suited to you).

scenarios.name: Differentiate TPD definition by life stage (own-occ primary earner / any-occ spouse)
scenarios.gate: Couple with differing work/earning situations (e.g. one on parental leave)
scenarios.strat: We recommend own-occupation TPD for the primary earner and retaining any-occupation TPD for the spouse who is currently out of the workforce / on parental leave.
scenarios.outcome: Cover definition is matched to each person's earning role and stage.
why: The primary earner's income is concentrated in a specific occupation (own-occupation is appropriate); the spouse currently out of the workforce is adequately served by the existing any-occupation cover, which is reviewed on return to work.
risks: Any-occupation has a higher claim hurdle; the spouse's cover should be reviewed and potentially upgraded on return to work.
alts: Own-occupation for both — higher cost not warranted while the spouse is out of the workforce.

scenarios.name: Trauma payout deployment (medical recovery + partner salary replacement)
scenarios.gate: Trauma cover recommended; sum insured sized to a purpose split
scenarios.strat: Your trauma cover is sized to cover an estimated amount for medical expenses plus an amount for your partner's salary replacement while you recover (e.g. $125,000 medical + the balance for partner salary replacement).
scenarios.outcome: The lump sum is explicitly sized to fund both your treatment/recovery costs and your partner's time off work to support you.
why: Segmenting the trauma sum insured into medical-recovery and partner-salary-replacement components ensures the household keeps running while you recover.
risks: The actual split needed may differ from the estimate; 'Plus' features may cap per condition.
alts: Standalone trauma plus separate income protection for the partner — duplicates cost.

scenarios.name: Retain cover during workforce absence (maternity / parental leave)
scenarios.gate: One person temporarily out of the workforce (e.g. parental leave)
scenarios.strat: While you are not working, we recommend you retain your existing in-super insurance cover (Life/TPD/IP) at its current levels, with the income protection structured with a shorter waiting period funded by available cash and leave, and we will reassess cover levels once you return to the workforce.
scenarios.outcome: Cover continuity is preserved through the leave period without re-underwriting, and is reviewed when income normalises.
why: Retaining cover during leave preserves your future insurability and avoids re-underwriting on return to work.
We are not recommending an increase in cover at this time given your cashflow while on leave; we will reassess once you have returned to work.
risks: You may be temporarily under-insured relative to your full needs analysis during the leave period; income protection may be limited while not earning.
alts: Cancel cover and re-apply on return — discounted due to re-underwriting cost, delay and the risk of a health change in the interim.

scenarios.name: Retain existing cover and top up with new cover
scenarios.gate: Transitional period (e.g. workforce re-entry) where flexibility is wanted
scenarios.strat: We recommend you retain your existing cover and top up with new recommended cover.
scenarios.outcome: You keep tax-effective in-super cover while adding flexible personal cover that can be adjusted later.
why: A small in-super retention is 'sticky' and tax-effective; the additional personal cover maintains optionality during a transitional period.
risks: Two policies mean more administration; the new cover must remain affordable after your circumstances settle.
alts: All new cover inside super — simpler but less flexible and locks in super deductions.

scenarios.name: Cancel cover no longer required (age + debt-free + income-replacement redundant)
scenarios.gate: Approaching/at retirement, debt cleared, no income to protect
scenarios.strat: By completing a full rollover of your existing super fund, your existing Life, TPD & Income Protection insurance will be cancelled. Due to your age and future lack of debt, we believe you do not require this or any other personal insurance going forward, and recommend you cancel your existing cover.
scenarios.outcome: Premiums no longer erode your balance once cover is no longer needed.
why: With no debt, no dependants relying on your income, and retirement income in place, personal insurance is no longer required, and cancelling it preserves your capital.
risks: If your circumstances change (e.g. new dependants), you may be unable to re-acquire cover at the same rates; ensure cover is genuinely no longer needed before cancelling.
alts: Retain partial cover via a partial rollover — discounted as it leaves more than one super account and ongoing premiums for cover you no longer require.

scenarios.name: Dual income protection — retail top-up over employer/industry cover (offset benefit)
scenarios.gate: Existing employer/industry-fund IP retained, with a retail policy added to top up
scenarios.strat: You will have two income protection policies (your existing fund cover plus the recommended retail policy). The retail policy is designed to top up the cover provided by your fund so that you receive up to 70% of your income. In the event of a claim you cannot receive the full benefit from both — the retail payout reduces by the amount paid from your fund cover.
scenarios.outcome: Your total income protection reaches ~70% of income at the lowest cost, by topping up rather than duplicating existing cover.
why: Retaining the existing fund cover and topping it up is cheaper than replacing it entirely.
Where the existing cover has no pre-existing medical exclusions, keeping it means a condition excluded on the new retail policy may still be claimable under the retained cover.
risks: The two policies overlap and benefits offset — you cannot stack both to exceed the insured percentage; coordination is required at claim time.
alts: Single standalone retail policy — simpler but more expensive and forfeits the no-exclusions benefit of the retained cover.

scenarios.name: Occupation pre-assessment / high-risk occupation constraint
scenarios.gate: Client in a high-risk / manual occupation affecting insurability
scenarios.strat: Given your occupation, an occupation pre-assessment was completed for this plan. As your role is considered high risk, the recommended insurer is the only one offering full benefits — other insurers either do not provide TPD/Income Protection or offer Income Protection with a shorter benefit period. Where your occupation caps cover (e.g. income protection limited to a set monthly amount, a shorter benefit period and no super contribution option), we have recommended cover within those limits.
scenarios.outcome: Your cover is placed with the insurer that will offer the fullest terms for your occupation, within the caps your occupation imposes.
why: High-risk occupations restrict insurer and product choice; a pre-assessment identifies the insurer offering the best available terms before you apply.
risks: Occupational caps may leave cover below your full needs (e.g. limited benefit period or monthly cap); review if you change occupation.
alts: Apply to a standard insurer — discounted as cover may be declined, loaded, or offered only with a reduced benefit period for your occupation.

scenarios.name: Size TPD sum insured with a super-tax uplift (gross-up if claimed in super)
scenarios.strat: The TPD sum insured is set to cover your identified needs plus an uplift (e.g. 22%) to cover the tax liability that would apply should you claim while the cover is held inside your superannuation fund.
scenarios.outcome: If you claim, the after-tax benefit still meets your identified needs because the sum insured was grossed up for the super tax.
why: A TPD benefit paid from super to a member under preservation age is taxed; grossing up the sum insured ensures the net benefit covers debts, costs and school fees as intended.
risks: If tax rates change the uplift may over- or under-compensate; the extra cover carries a small additional premium; if cover were held outside super this tax would not apply.
alts: Hold TPD outside super (no benefits tax, but premiums are not funded from super) or take cover without the uplift (net benefit reduced by tax).

scenarios.name: Income Protection affordability structuring — waiting & benefit period calibrated to cash/leave
scenarios.strat: We have recommended a 90-day waiting period as you have available cash and leave to fund 90 days of expenses, which reduces the overall cost of the cover. The benefit period is set to balance coverage and cost — the longest available where maximum protection is wanted, or a shorter (e.g. 2-year) benefit period where cash and leave reserves can bridge a longer absence.
scenarios.outcome: Your income protection cost is minimised by matching the waiting and benefit periods to the reserves you already hold.
why: A longer waiting period and/or shorter benefit period lowers the premium; this is appropriate where you hold sufficient cash and leave to self-fund the gap.
risks: A longer wait or shorter benefit period leaves you self-funding longer — vulnerable if your cash/leave is depleted (e.g. redundancy alongside disability) or a disability extends beyond the benefit period.
alts: Shorter waiting period (e.g. 30 days) and/or benefit period to age 65 — maximum security at a higher premium.

scenarios.name: Retain, alter and/or cancel a mix of existing covers (retain X / cancel Y / alter Z)
scenarios.strat: We recommend you retain [cover X], cancel [cover Y] and alter [cover Z] across your existing policies as set out below.
why: Tailors your existing cover to current needs without wholesale replacement.

scenarios.name: Any-occupation TPD definition
scenarios.strat: We recommend TPD cover on an Any-Occupation definition.
why: Any-Occupation is more affordable than Own-Occupation; appropriate where own-occupation is not available or not warranted.

scenarios.name: Non-occupational / homemaker TPD definition
scenarios.strat: We recommend TPD cover on a Non-Occupational (homemaker) definition, appropriate as you are not currently in the workforce.
why: Provides TPD protection for a non-working person where occupation-based definitions don't apply.

scenarios.name: Transfer existing cover to the recommended platform via takeover terms + top up with new cover
scenarios.strat: We recommend transferring your existing [industry-fund] cover to the recommended platform via takeover terms, and topping up with new recommended cover through the product insurer.
why: Takeover terms preserve your existing cover (and avoid new exclusions identified at pre-assessment) while the top-up provides the additional cover you need.
risks: Takeover terms have conditions; the new top-up cover is separately underwritten and may carry exclusions or loadings.

scenarios.name: Pre-assessment factors (smoker / health / pastimes) affecting terms
scenarios.strat: Note: based on pre-assessment of your [smoker status / health / pastimes], the recommended insurer offers the best available terms; cover may be subject to loadings or exclusions.
